doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: How African-American rhythm differs: dotted eighth notes
summary: Roker explains that the same notes feel different when played with a dotted, blues or Afro-Cuban feeling.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You know jazz, what kind of separates jazz from other forms of music, like European classical music, is the vitality and the pervasive nature of rhythm. Could you elaborate on that and tell us how that rhythm is different in, particularly in the African-American community and in the way it enunciates jazz, than rhythm in other styles of music or other cultures.

Well an eighth note is an eighth note, but it’s the way the eighth notes are played. Some people play ‘em like [claps]. But in the Afro community, it’s [claps] it’s dotted. That’s the whole difference. And if you can play with that type of feeling instilled in the rhythm then you have the blues and then you have Afro-Cuban all at the same time. Because they play [claps]. You hear the six-eight? And then the shuffle. [claps] And that’s the only difference, is— because the notes are the same but it’s the way you play the notes. And it’s just a feeling that you have to have. It’s hard for me to explain a feeling. I’m not, you know, it’s something that you have to do you know. And somebody has to teach you how to do it.
